newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Top bankers held as Vietnam debt scandal widens.
newsitem.headline: Top bankers held as Vietnam debt scandal widens.

text.p: Banking officials in Ho Chi Minh City said on Monday that police had detained seven senior banking executives in the latest twist to a debt scandal surrounding two of Vietnam's largest conglomerates.
The officials said that the five senior Incombank employees and two executives from the country's biggest state-owned bank, Vietcombank, were arrested on Saturday.
They declined to give details, but local newspapers said all seven had been charged with "violating state regulations on economic management causing serious consequences".
The arrests were the latest in a widening scandal surrounding debt-crippled firms Minh Phung and EPCO, whose directors were detained in March and subsequently charged with fraud.
More than 20 others have been arrested since then in a case whose scale and repercussions are continuing to emerge.

Minh Phung, a garments-to-property conglomerate, defaulted on loans of about $17.1 million from Vietcombank. Those loans were secured with steel and other commodities that were "borrowed" from EPCO but turned out to have been already sold.
However, that was only a fraction of Minh Phung's total debts, put by state media at some $370 million and said to have been largely run up by failed speculation in the property market.
State-owned Incombank is owed the bulk of that sum.

In a gruesome twist to the saga, a senior Minh Phung executive and former Vietcombank employee, Nguyen Van Ha, was found dead in at Incombank's Ho Chi Minh City headquarters last month. His head was attached by metal wire to an electrical circuit board.
The official Saigon Giai Phong newspaper said the five Incombank officials were accused of helping Minh Phung secure huge loans by deliberately overstating the value of mortgaged assets.

The two Vietcombank executives, who were suspended earlier this month, are said to have failed to inspect the value of Minh Phung-mortgaged assets, thereby allowing the firm to expropriate some $11 million through 13 credit contracts with the bank.

Vietnam, which launched free-market reforms in the late 1980s, has been hit by a string of high-profile corruption and economic scandals this year, dealing a blow to confidence and sending shock waves throughout the country's arcane political system.
Earlier this year, a Ho Chi Minh City court sentenced four people to death and jailed more than a dozen in connection with corruption at Communist Party-affiliated trading firm Tamexco.
The Saigon Times Daily said on Monday that officials at several party organisations, including the financial management board of Ho Chi Minh City's Party Unit were being disciplined over the affair.
